title: Limited Protest of American Electric Power Service Corporation to PJM Interconnection, LLC’s proposed revisions to the Open Access Transmission Tariff and Reliability Assurance Agreement Among Load Serving Entities under ER26-3380.

documents.name: Final_AEP Protest_Docket No. ER26-3380.pdf
documents.text:
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                  BEFORE THE
                    FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

PJM Interconnection, LLC                               )               Docket No. ER26-3380-000

                            LIMITED PROTEST OF
               AMERICAN ELECTRIC POWER SERVICE CORPORATION

       Pursuant to Rule 211 of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (“Commission”)

Rules of Practice and Procedure,1 American Electric Power Service Corporation, on behalf of its

affiliates Appalachian Power Company, Indiana Michigan Power Company, Kentucky Power

Company, Kingsport Power Company, Ohio Power Company, Wheeling Power Company, AEP

Appalachian Transmission Company, Inc., AEP Indiana Michigan Transmission Company, Inc.,

AEP Kentucky Transmission Company, Inc., AEP Ohio Transmission Company, Inc., and AEP

West Virginia Transmission Company, Inc. (collectively, “AEP”), hereby submits this protest to

PJM Interconnection, LLC’s (“PJM”) proposed revisions to its Open Access Transmission Tariff

(“Tariff”) and Reliability Assurance Agreement Among Load Serving Entities (“RAA”) to

establish a Reliability Backstop Procurement (“RBP”) to Address Resource Adequacy Concerns

Stemming from Large Loads.2

I.     EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

       The resource adequacy crisis in PJM is undisputed. PJM is confronting the most significant

generation need in its history. Demand from national security needs, advanced manufacturing,

data centers, and electrification is accelerating faster than PJM’s current interconnection processes




1
       18 C.F.R. §§ 385.211, 385.214 (2025).
2
         Reliability Backstop Procurement to Address Resource Adequacy Concerns Stemming from New Load
Adjustments, Docket No. ER26-3380 (filed July 31, 2026) (“RBP Proposal”). AEP filed a doc-less motion to
intervene in the captioned docket on August 5, 2026.
 and market mechanisms allow the region to plan and build the infrastructure needed to reliably

support such unprecedented load growth. Given the urgency of the problem, PJM rightfully

proposes to move with extraordinary speed to commit significant capital to new generating

capacity. AEP has urged PJM to aggressively address both the current resource adequacy crisis

and the existing structures that gave rise to the shortfall, and supports measures to address the PJM

region’s capacity shortfall. Notwithstanding AEP’s support for swift and decisive action, the

amount of capital required for this effort and the associated potential impact on wholesale and

retail rates render the details of implementation critically important. With that in mind, several

important elements of the RBP Proposal must be reformed to ensure that the RBP produces just

and reasonable outcomes for customers. Consequently, AEP urges the Commission to exercise

caution, subject the RBP Proposal’s details to meaningful scrutiny, and make use of the broad

discretion PJM has afforded the Commission through its willingness to make the components of

the RBP design “severable” for purposes of NRG.3

        Despite AEP’s overall support for the RBP concept as a near-term measure to address the

region’s resource adequacy crisis, certain changes are needed. Specifically, the Commission

should: (1) either reject PJM’s proposed Transmission Owner4 exit provisions or direct PJM to

modify them to limit any continuing RBP financial obligation of a departing Transmission Owner

to the RBP Charges already allocated to that Transmission Owner’s zone under the Commission-

accepted RBP Charge cost allocation methodology, and confirm that any new provisions do not

disturb the Commission’s established precedent governing Regional Transmission Operator

clarify that: (a) Electric Distributors bear no financial liability for RBP Charges solely by virtue

of their administrative role to report Load Serving Entities’ (“LSEs’”) RBP Obligations; and (b)

collateral obligations attach to LSEs allocated RBP Charges; and (3) direct PJM to acknowledge

and correct on compliance the drafting error in RAA, Schedule 8.1.D, Section D.1.1 that would,

as written, fail to achieve PJM’s stated intent with respect to Fixed Resource Requirement (“FRR”)

Entities.

 III.    BACKGROUND

        To address the near-term reliability concerns exposed by PJM’s 2028/2029 Base Residual

Auction (“BRA”), which cleared short of PJM’s target reserve margin by 6,831.3 MW at the

Commission-approved price cap of $325/MW-day, PJM proposes to conduct a one-time RBP for

procuring new capacity from September 30, 2026 to October 21, 2026.6 The proposed rules

governing the RBP are set forth in PJM’s Tariff and PJM’s RAA and are designed to allow PJM

to procure the capacity needed to meet the shortfall from the 2028/2029 BRA.7 The January 16,

2026 National Energy Dominance Council/PJM Governors’ Principles urged PJM to procure new

capacity through a backstop auction commencing no later than September 2026, provide 15-year

price certainty for new capacity resources, and allocate the costs of that capacity to LSEs with new

data centers that have not self-procured new capacity or agreed to be curtailable.8 PJM explains

that the initial RBP procurement target (“Initial Target”) for the RBP will be set at 6,831.3 MW,

subject to reduction after PJM has accounted for certain self-supplied new capacity and opt-outs.9

        Noting that PJM members have expressed a strong preference for bringing new capacity to

the PJM system voluntarily rather than contracting through PJM, PJM has facilitated a bilateral

matching process to connect new capacity with new load. The process began with an RFP on June

         PJM explains that offers in the RBP will be for a fixed 15-year Delivery Year term and are

expected to commence commercial operation in the 2028/2029 Delivery Year.13 RBP capacity

will be paid-as-bid and subject to a must-offer requirement for the term of its commitment.14 The

a set of resources that does not match the Final Target.17

According to PJM, “including locational parameters based on today’s conditions would . . . lead

        Each committed RBP Resource will individually settle as a contract-for-differences

(“CfD”).23 This settlement structure turns on a committed RBP Resource’s individualized strike

price. A committed RBP Resource must offer all committed RBP Unforced Capacity (“UCAP”)

MW as a price-taker in the RPM, unless a qualifying exception applies. The market price for the

RBP Resource is specifically defined as the resource’s unit-specific weighted average resource

clearing price (“WARCP”) for all RPM Auctions in which the RBP Resource participated for the

       PJM proposes a three-tiered cost allocation system for RBP Charges, first allocating costs

to Electric Distributor zones/areas, followed by LSEs, and then ultimately to retail customers. For

the last two steps, PJM’s cost allocation methodology relies on coordination between Electric

Distributor zones/areas, state regulatory authorities, and state regulatory processes. First, before

allocating RBP Charges, PJM allocates cost responsibility to the relevant Electric Distributor

zones/areas. To do so, PJM proposes to determine each relevant Electric Distributor zone/area’s

pro rata responsibility for the Initial Target based on forecasted load growth from the 2026/2027

Delivery Year to the 2028/2029 Delivery Year, incorporating certain load adjustments from the

2026 PJM Load Forecast.27 PJM then proposes to adjust each Electric Distributor zone/area’s

allocation to reflect reductions based on its ability to procure Qualifying Offset MWs or

successfully support an opt-out.28 After calculating the Final Target, PJM will reallocate RBP

After receiving its allocation of RBP Charges, each Electric Distributor will coordinate with states

and/or the Relevant Electric Retail Regulatory Authority (“RERRA”) to determine the allocation

If no RBP Obligation is reported, PJM will assign RBP Charges to LSEs using PJM’s method for

allocating capacity costs pursuant to RAA, Schedule 8.31 Finally, states and RERRAs may decide

how to further allocate RBP Charges to the appropriate retail customers.32

       RBP Buyers and Sellers must meet a variety of requirements to become eligible to

participate in the RBP, including collateral requirements that apply in addition to and separate

from existing collateral requirements.33 RBP Buyers are required to post collateral to mitigate the

PJM first determines the overall credit requirement needed to address the risk associated with RBP

commitments throughout the RBP 15-year term on a region-wide basis, assigning a $/MW rate

applicable to all RBP capacity.35 In determining the credit requirement, PJM will multiply the

total capacity committed in the RBP by the RBP Credit Rate, which is initially set at $1.5 million.36

         PJM also proposes rules setting forth the responsibilities of “various parties” in the event

IV.     PROTEST

        A.       PJM’s Proposed Transmission Owner Exit Provisions are Unjust and
                 Unreasonable

        The RBP Proposal, absent the modifications requested herein, could meaningfully and

unfairly expand the negotiated terms of exit embedded in the Consolidated Transmission Owner’s

Agreement (“TO Agreement”), Operating Agreement (“OA”) and RAA. If and to the extent the

Commission approves the RBP, AEP does not object to the notion that departing loads continue

to pay for the RBP Charges assigned to them as a result of this one-time event, but objects to the

imposition of an exit fee that obligates departing load to pay for charges that are unrelated to its

fair allocation of RBP commitments.

        AEP has publicly announced that it is evaluating whether continued membership in PJM

will be in the best interest of its customers in the long run. It is common knowledge that PJM’s

         Id. at 92-94. PJM states that the exact amount that an exiting Transmission Owner would owe would be
determined through a separate filing with the Commission. Id. at 94. Thereafter, PJM states that it would pay the
collected revenues from the Transmission Owner to the impacted RBP Resources as payments become due. Id.
43
        NRG, 862 F.3d 108.
44
         RBP Proposal at 3. PJM cautions that if severance or modification gives rise to complications, it may delay
the opening of the RBP procurement window, causing downstream impacts such as the need to delay the BRA for the
2029/2030 Delivery Year. Id.
                                                        10
 governing documents do not contain an exit fee, and Commission precedent confirms that a

departing member’s obligation with regard to generating capacity charges extend only through the

last RPM auction in which that departing member’s load was included. With that in mind, the

RBP Proposal’s exit provisions stand to broaden what the Commission has deemed necessary for

departing load to honor cost commitments.                  Principles of cost causation require PJM to

demonstrate a reasonable nexus between the capacity procured in the RBP and the reliability need

for which customers are being charged. As drafted, the RBP Proposal would impose a financial

obligation on a departing Transmission Owner based not on the RBP Charges allocated to an

Electric Distributor zone/area pursuant to PJM’s proposed RBP cost allocation methodology, but

on where PJM happens to procure or locate new RBP resources. In this respect, the RBP Proposal

flouts cost causation principles by imposing an exit fee that could far exceed the RBP Charges

allocated to a departing Transmission Owner’s zone.45

        For these reasons and as explained further below, the Commission should reject the

proposed Transmission Owner exit provisions or, at minimum, require PJM to revise them before

acceptance. Any revised exit provisions should be consistent with these principles: (1) a departing

Transmission Owner’s responsibility for RBP Charges is limited to the RBP Charges otherwise

assigned to its zone/area under the Commission-accepted RBP cost allocation; (2) PJM may not

require a departing Transmission Owner to assume or guarantee, payment of obligations associated

with RBP Resources beyond that limited responsibility, nor require acceleration of any payment

obligation; (3) any proposed RTO replacement arrangement or continuity agreement must be

calculated by reference to the withdrawing Transmission Owner’s allocated RBP Charges, not by

that all approved rates reflect to some degree the costs actually caused by the customer who pays them).

 artificial reference to RBP Resources physically located in the relevant zone; (4) a Transmission

Owner’s responsibility for RBP Charges should remain eligible for the RBP Settlement Credits

and RPM Auction Credits that would apply as cost offsets if the same load remained in PJM; and

(5) the exit fee attributable to a departing Transmission Owner’s responsibility for RBP Charges

should be reasonably capable of being calculated with the information known based on the results

of the RBP.

                 1.       The Proposed Exit Terms Lack Sufficient Clarity and Detail

         The RBP Proposal’s proposed allocation of RBP Charges to departing Transmission

Owners, first of all, lacks needed detail in light of the enormity of the financial burden it stands to

impose. Moreover, even the language that is sufficiently clear creates an unjust and unreasonable

obligation on a withdrawing member.

         Specifically, section 18.7 of the proposed Tariff language lacks administrable standards

and is underdeveloped for the following reasons:

     •   Section 18.7 (a) first mentions voluntary agreements that a departing Transmission Owner

         “may” enter into with RBP Resources in the applicable zone under the standard that they

         “preserve[] the RBP commitments . . . with the owners of RBP Resources . . . .”46 It is not

         clear what this standard requires, including whether that agreement is intended to preserve

         that unit’s obligations to PJM, or whether the RBP Resource could agree to serve as a

         capacity resource to the departing Transmission Owner.

     •   PJM also has not explained or justified its request to have unfettered discretion to merely

         elect not to “retain” an RBP Resource that can be pseudo-tied back to PJM, as provided in




46
         RBP Proposal, Attachment B, Clean Tariff Records, Attachment DD, § 18.7(a) (“Proposed Tariff”).
                                                      12
          section 18.7(a).47 Pursuant to the second paragraph of section 18.7(a), PJM wants the right

         to “elect” not to retain such a resource that could be pseudo-tied and foist a financial

         obligation on the departing member to take on 100 percent of the RBP Resource’s

         remaining revenue requirement for the 15-year term.48

     •   Section 18.7(b) in turn is also fatally vague. It provides that a departing Transmission

         Owner exiting with net load that has been allocated RBP Charges for RBP Resources not

         located in its zone should enter into bilateral contracts with RBP resource not located in

         its Zone—i.e., with resources remaining in PJM—under the vague notion that such an

         agreement would “preserve[] the RBP commitments.”49 Since a departing Transmission

         Owner will have no relationship with any such unit, it is not clear what sort of contract may

         satisfy this requirement.

                  2.      The Proposed Exit Terms are Unjust and Unreasonable Because the
                          RBP Charges of Departing Zones Are Not Reduced By
                          Corresponding RPM Revenues or Other Offsets

         PJM’s proposed exit provisions are also unjust and unreasonable because they: (1) appear

to require a departing Electric Distributor zone/area to assume liability for the gross cost of RBP

Resources without preserving the offsets and settlement protections that would apply if the same

load remained in PJM; and (2) do not protect departing Transmission Owners from assuming RBP

Charges in the event that RBP Resource capacity becomes surplus in PJM. Under PJM’s proposed

CfD structure, RBP Buyers pay RBP Charges based not simply on the full quantity of RBP MW

acquired, but rather on an adjusted value that reflects a corresponding settlement value from PJM.

 Under PJM’s proposed exit structure, however, departing load appears to be required to fund the

full RBP strike price without the adjustment afforded to remaining members.

       The RBP Charge is intended to be netted against the resource’s RPM market value through

the offsetting the RBP Settlement Credit, which is based on the lesser of three MW values: (1)

daily committed RBP UCAP MWs, (2) daily owned UCAP MWs, and (3) daily cleared RPM

UCAP MWs.50 That offset is central to PJM’s own explanation of the RBP as a supplement to,

not a replacement for, RPM.51 However, PJM’s proposed Transmission Owner withdrawal

provisions only provide that a Transmission Owner departing with net load that has been allocated

RBP Charges for RBP Resources—if it does not enter into agreements that maintain appropriate

rates, terms and conditions that preserve the RBP commitments with the owners of such RBP

Resources—must pay all forward obligations on an accelerated basis through the remaining term

of the RBP commitment.52 This proposed term does not make clear that a Transmission Owner

departing with net load and responsible for funding RBP commitments throughout their 15-year

commitment term would be afforded the offset price for an RBP Resource that it would receive if

it stayed in PJM.

       In the example provided by PJM, the RBP Resource may clear substantially more MWs in

the RBP than in the RPM, but is still eligible to receive RBP Settlement Credits that reduce the

RBP Charge assessed.53 If a Transmission Owner’s post-exit obligation is calculated based only

on the gross RBP Charge, while disregarding the quantity of RBP MW that clears both the RBP

and RPM, the exit fee allocated to an exiting Transmission Owner would be calculated without

 accounting for the offsets that would otherwise accrue had it stayed in PJM. Consequently,

departing Transmission Owners and their load remain exposed to a substantial portion of the RBP

Charges with no corresponding opportunity to receive an offset to the RBP Charge, thus forcing

the departing Transmission Owner and its customers to pay more than similarly situated load that

stays in PJM. This result is unjust, unreasonable, and unduly discriminatory, and is not tied to cost

causation.

       This outcome is asymmetrical and inconsistent with PJM’s stated premise that RPM

remains the foundational capacity market and that the RBP merely addresses incremental resource

adequacy concerns. If a Transmission Owner departing with load is required to fund the entire

RBP payment obligation for an RBP Resource, principles of cost causation require that departing

load should receive a corresponding RPM Auction Credit or RBP Settlement Credit tied to the full

amount of capacity for which it is paying. Otherwise, the RBP would function less as a

supplemental reliability mechanism and more as an additional capacity procurement obligation

requiring load to pay a higher RBP Charge for the RBP Resources in its zone than it would have

otherwise been assessed had the load stayed in PJM. The Commission should direct PJM to

explain why this outcome fairly represents a Transmission Owner’s responsibility for its RBP

Charges.

       PJM should also be required to demonstrate why it proposes to limit the RBP Settlement

Credit to overlapping RPM-cleared MW only for load remaining in PJM, and how that limitation

produces a just and reasonable allocation of RBP Charges and benefits for departing Transmission

Owners or Electric Distributor zones/areas. This design increases the risk that a departing

Transmission Owner will be allocated an unreasonable share of RBP Charges following its

withdrawal from PJM. The examples put forth in the RBP Proposal illustrate that the economic


                                                 15
 value of the CfD is limited to the quantity of MW that clears in both RPM and the RBP. 54 This

limitation becomes particularly significant in the event that future load reductions, market changes,

or an Electric Distributor or Transmission Owner exit result in RBP Resources becoming surplus

to PJM’s capacity needs. For example—and as a result of PJM’s decision not to implement

locational parameters in the RBP—if a Transmission Owner leaves PJM with the net load that

formed the basis for its allocation of RBP Charges, the RBP Resources procured on its behalf that

are located outside of the zone/area may no longer be needed in PJM. Under such circumstances,

RPM clearing levels may decline, thereby reducing or eliminating the quantity of MW eligible for

CfD settlement and associated RBP Settlement Credits or RPM Auction Credits, while customers

in the exiting zones/areas remain responsible for the underlying RBP Charges. The RBP Proposal

therefore creates the possibility that departing load will continue paying for RBP Resources long

after the market no longer recognizes equivalent capacity value through RPM.

       This is especially concerning with respect to PJM’s proposed long-term cost responsibility

framework. If an Electric Distributor or Transmission Owner remains responsible for RBP

Charges after an exit, PJM has not demonstrated that corresponding RPM revenues or CfD

settlement benefits, including RPM Auction Credits and RBP Settlement Credits, will remain

available throughout the 15-year commitment. The RBP Proposal therefore risks creating an

unfairly fixed financial obligation under which customers remain responsible for unabated RBP

Charges, even as the quantity of RBP MW eligible to receive RPM Auction Credits declines over

time. At a minimum, PJM should clarify how withdrawing Transmission Owners will be protected

from paying for RBP Resources whose capacity has become surplus to PJM’s needs and no longer

other changes in conditions impacting resource adequacy in PJM.

                      3.   Any Imposed Exit Terms Should Be Consistent with Cost Causation
                           And Should be Capable of Determination in Advance of Withdrawal

         In addition to the issues addressed above, the RBP Proposal reflects a disconnect between

a departing load’s responsibility for RBP Charges upon withdrawal and PJM’s proposed exit

charges without explanation regarding how the proposed exit fee is tied to the departing load’s

initial allocation of RBP Charges. The starting point for this analysis is PJM’s decision to propose

an RBP process with no locational deliverability requirement.55 The RBP Proposal expressly

assumes that new generation anywhere in PJM is deliverable to any load in PJM. Under its

proposal, PJM could acquire all 6,831.3 MW of new supply in New Jersey, or North Carolina, or

even suburban Chicago. More to the point for AEP, PJM could decide to acquire all—or at least

a disproportionate share of — the new capacity in Ohio. This is a stark departure from the RPM’s

design, which does include locational elements, and relies on Capacity Emergency Transfer

Objectives (“CETO”) and Capacity Emergency Transfer Limits (“CETL”) modeling to ensure that

cleared capacity can address the reliability needs of constrained areas. 56 As a result, customers

may be required to fund RBP Resources that are not deliverable to their zone, while resources that

are necessary to address local reliability needs may not be procured at all. The RBP Proposal

zone/area. Thus, if PJM procures a substantial amount of RBP capacity in one zone/area, the

Transmission Owner for that zone/area could face exit-related obligations materially greater than

those imposed by the RBP Charges otherwise allocated to that zone/area. PJM’s potentially

punitive proposal threatens to place an undue burden on departing Transmission Owners solely by

virtue of where RBP Resources are located. This outcome would create an undue barrier to a

Transmission Owner’s ability to exercise its long-held contractual right to leave.

expand the contractual requirements on Transmission Owners seeking to withdraw from PJM.

Stated differently, PJM’s proposed exit framework could transform each LSE’s allocated RBP

Charge into an unduly burdensome exit fee for a departing Transmission Owner. The Commission

should reject the proposed exit provisions and require PJM to limit a departing Transmission

Owner’s liability to the RBP Charges allocated to its zone under PJM’s proposed cost allocation

methodology, as accepted by the Commission. Modifying PJM’s proposal in this manner would

calculated using the information known once the RBP results are final. The cost of exiting an RTO

must be clear and transparent so that a Transmission Owner can act in the best interests of its

customers. As stated above, the formula should begin with the departing Transmission Owner’s

zone or area-level’s allocation of RBP Charges established under a Commission-accepted cost

allocation for RBP Charges, as adjusted for any Qualifying RBP Offset MW, opt-outs, or other

accepted reductions.    That amount should then be converted into a fixed, annual payment

obligation for each remaining Delivery Year of the RBP commitment term, based on the RBP

should be reduced by any RBP Settlement Credits, RPM Auction Credits, refunds, offsets, or other

credits that would have applied had the load remained in PJM, and it should not include any

       B.     PJM’s Proposed Cost Allocation Methodology Is Not Just and Reasonable
              And Requires Further Development

       Given the amount of customer funding the RBP Proposal could require, ensuring a just and

reasonable and not unduly discriminatory cost allocation of RBP Charges is of paramount

importance. As proposed, the cost allocation terms included in the RBP Proposal leave key

questions unanswered. First, PJM’s proposed location-based cost allocation methodology is at

odds with its decision not to include locational parameters in the RBP. Second, PJM’s use of a

single load forecast as the basis for 15-years of cost allocation is unreasonable absent some

allowance for adjustment to allocation over time. Third, the proposed provisions require further

development to ensure that Electric Distributors are not left responsible for an unreasonable

allocation of RBP Charges.

                  1.       PJM’s Static Load-Forecast Cost Allocation Is Unjust and
                          Unreasonable Because It Disconnects Long-Term RBP Charges From
                          Actual Load Responsibility

        PJM proposes to allocate RBP Charges by first imputing the current 6,831.3 MW shortfall

to each Electric Distributor zone/area based in part on that zone/area’s forecasted load growth from

the 2026/2027 Delivery Year to the 2028/2029 Delivery Year.89 PJM’s proposal to use the

forecasted load growth between those Delivery Years to allocate a financial obligation that will

run through the 2042/2043 Delivery Year creates a number of problems. First, PJM’s proposal to

allocate costs based on zonal responsibility for its current reliability shortfall is at odds with its

concession that there will be no locational element to the RBP. PJM’s theory that its load forecast

is a reliable proxy for where in the PJM region the resource adequacy shortfall exists, paired with

its decision not to include a locational element to capacity procurement, creates a fundamental

disconnect between the product procured and the allocation of RBP Charges for the product. For

example, load in western PJM may end up paying for significant new generation investments in

eastern PJM that ultimately do not benefit that western load, or vice versa.

        Second, the temporal mismatch created by the RBP Proposal is independently

unreasonable. PJM proposes to allocate a 15-year stream of RBP Charges through the 2042/2043

Delivery Year using a single snapshot of relative load growth between the 2026/2027 and

2028/2029 Delivery Years, even though load growth patterns are highly likely to shift materially

over that period as large-load projects, interconnection timelines, retirements, and customer

commitments change. PJM acknowledges that it cannot project CETO and CETL 15 years out

because it lacks the information needed to determine those locational parameters. PJM cannot

               2.      PJM’s Cost Allocation Provisions Must be Further Clarified to Avoid
                       Placing Unreasonable Burdens on Electric Distributors

       The proposed provisions governing cost allocation to LSEs—i.e., the parties taking

transmission service on behalf of the large load customer in question—require further development

to ensure that Electric Distributors are not left responsible for an undue allocation of RBP Charges.

Unlike PJM’s allocation of RBP Charges to Electric Distributor areas/zones, which will be set to

a fixed amount and assigned by PJM, the proposed allocation of RBP Charges to LSEs is much

less definitive, thereby exposing Electric Distributors to risk for assuming unwarranted RBP costs.

       According to the RBP Proposal, after PJM allocates RBP Charges to each Electric

Distributor zone/area, those RBP Charges will be further allocated to each LSE based on the LSE’s

pro-rata share of the zone’s RBP Obligation. This allocation depends entirely on actions by parties

that neither PJM nor the Electric Distributor can compel. Although PJM’s proposal nominally

places payment obligations on LSEs rather than Electric Distributors, the practical reality is more

complex. The Electric Distributor is the entity responsible for a host of administrative functions

that will impact on how costs are allocated among LSEs according to their pro-rata share of their

zone using each LSE’s load ratio share of the Daily Unforced Capacity Obligation for the zone as

determined in Schedule 8 of the RAA. Importantly, PJM’s proposal also does not mention which

party bears responsibility if LSEs decide not to pay their allocated share of RBP Charges or if their

load commitments shift over time, or if an LSE disputes their previously-allocated share of RBP

Charges. Given that the Electric Distributors zones/areas are assigned a fixed amount of RBP

Charges that will be expressly defined by the Tariff, the ambiguities regarding LSEs’

responsibilities for RBP Charges leave Electric Distributors at a significant disadvantage for

bearing costs that, by design, should be allocated fairly among responsible LSEs before ultimately

being allocated to load. This outcome would be consistent with both the design of the RBP and

the Trump Administration’s Ratepayer Protection Pledge.90

zone/area in which that customer happens to be located. If the purpose of the RBP is to ensure

the corresponding RBP obligation transfers to the successor LSE serving that same load. That

given Delivery Year must post credit associated with that obligation. PJM must clarify that

collateral obligations attach only to LSEs allocated responsibility for RBP Charges, not to Electric

Distributors acting solely in an administrative or delivery-service role. PJM expressly states that

RBP Buyer collateral is intended to protect against the risk that an entity responsible for RBP

Charges fails to pay those charges. This collateral obligation should therefore follow the entity

ultimately responsible for the RBP Charge. Given that LSEs are the parties taking transmission

service on behalf of the large loads that have caused the need for the RBP, the burden to acquire

collateral should reside with the LSE.


                                                 32
        The Commission should direct PJM to clarify that the obligation to post RBP Collateral

applies exclusively to LSEs allocated responsibility for RBP Charges and does not attach to an

Electric Distributor solely because the applicable load is located within its distribution service

territory. PJM explains that RBP Buyer collateral is intended to mitigate the risk of non-payment

of RBP Charges and that only LSEs allocated responsibility for RBP Charges generally will have

a credit requirement. The RBP Proposal therefore appears to recognize that collateral should

follow financial responsibility for RBP Charges. Given the substantial magnitude and long

duration of the proposed collateral requirements, however, the Tariff should expressly state that

Electric Distributors have no obligation to post RBP Collateral unless they are serving the

underlying load in their capacity as an LSE.         Failure to provide such clarification creates

unnecessary uncertainty regarding which market participants ultimately bear the financial

obligations associated with the RBP framework.

       This clarification is also necessary to ensure consistency with the cost-causation principles

that PJM invokes throughout the filing. PJM’s proposed cost allocation methodology is premised

on assigning RBP Charges to the LSEs serving the load that gives rise to the resource adequacy

need underlying the RBP. It would therefore be inconsistent and unreasonable to require an

Electric Distributor, whose role in the RBP framework is limited to delivery service and

administrative reporting of allocations, to provide collateral backing obligations incurred by

competitive suppliers serving that load. This concern is particularly acute in the AEP Ohio Electric

Distributor zone/area, where essentially all large-load and data center customers driving forecasted

load growth are shopping customers served by competitive retail suppliers acting as LSEs.

Requiring AEP Ohio to post collateral for obligations attributable to those suppliers would

improperly shift credit risk from the entities serving and benefiting from the load to an Electric


                                                33
 Distributor that neither controls generation supply decisions nor receives the revenues associated

with serving that load. Such a result would be inconsistent with cost-causation principles and

should be expressly foreclosed in the Tariff.

       The Commission should therefore direct PJM to modify the RBP Tariff language to

expressly state that, “RBP Collateral shall be required only of those Load Serving Entities allocated

responsibility for RBP Charges pursuant to Attachment DD. An Electric Distributor shall have no

obligation to post RBP Collateral solely by virtue of serving as the Electric Distributor for a zone

or area, except to the extent the Electric Distributor is also acting as the Load Serving Entity for

the applicable load.”

       D.      PJM’s Proposal Contains an Error Regarding Fixed Resource Requirement
               Entities That Must Be Addressed

       The RBP Proposal contains an error that, if the Commission accepts the RBP Proposal, the

Commission should direct PJM to amend on compliance. In RAA, Schedule 8, Article 1, Section

D 1.1, PJM proposes language stating that “An FRR Entity may not use an Existing Generation

Capacity Resource not owned by such FRR Entity as of June 1, 2027 or any resource committed

through the Reliability Backstop Procurement to satisfy its Capacity FRR Plan.”91 This mistake,

lacking the ability to use both owned or contracted resources, if accepted, would represent a critical

error in the filed rate as applied to FRR Entities. In conversations with PJM since the RBP

Proposal was submitted, PJM has conceded to AEP that this mistake was a simple drafting error.

Consequently, PJM must acknowledge this error on the record of this proceeding and commit to

fixing it in a compliance filing.

 V.      CONCLUSION

        AEP recognizes that PJM faces a genuine and pressing resource adequacy challenge and

does not oppose a carefully tailored one-time backstop procurement designed to address the

2028/2029 BRA shortfall. That said, the extraordinary speed, cost, and duration of the RBP

Proposal require the Commission to scrutinize the proposed terms carefully before customers are

exposed to billions of dollars in long-term financial commitments. As explained in this Protest,

the RBP Proposal contains provisions that are unjust, unreasonable, and unduly discriminatory.

AEP therefore respectfully requests that the Commission reject those provisions of the RBP

Proposal or, at minimum, condition any acceptance of the RBP Proposal on the modifications and

clarifications described above.

        Specifically, the Commission should:

     1. Reject or direct PJM to substantially revise the RBP Proposal’s Transmission Owner exit

        provisions to: (a) ensure that a departing Transmission Owner’s financial obligation for

        RBP Charges is limited to the charges allocated to its zone under PJM’s Commission-

        accepted RBP cost allocation methodology, subject to reduction by any RBP Settlement

        Credits, RPM Auction Credits, refunds, offsets, or other credits that would have applied

        had the load remained in PJM; and (b) make the cost of exiting PJM transparent and readily

        ascertainable through an objective, pre-determinable formula;

     2. Reaffirm the Commission’s established precedent governing RTO exit obligations, and

        expressly confirm that any RBP exit obligation accepted in this proceeding is confined to

        RBP Charges and does not disturb, expand, or supersede the contractual exit framework

        established in Duquesne I and II and related orders, including the absence of any general

        PJM exit fee;


                                                35
    3. Reject or direct PJM to modify the proposed RBP cost allocation methodology by: (a)

       expressly stating that Electric Distributors bear no financial liability for RBP Charges

       solely by virtue of their administrative role in reporting LSE RBP Obligations; (b)

       providing that collateral obligations attach exclusively to LSEs allocated responsibility for

       RBP Charges and not to Electric Distributors acting in a delivery-service or reporting

       capacity; and (c) adopting a mechanism to revisit cost allocation over the 15-year RBP

       commitment term as actual load and reliability conditions evolve; and

   4. Direct PJM to correct the identified drafting error in RAA, Schedule 8.1.D, Section

       D.1.1 affecting FRR Entities on compliance, and to acknowledge that error on the record

       of this proceeding.

       These conditions are necessary to ensure that any one-time backstop procurement approved

by the Commission addresses PJM’s asserted reliability need without imposing unjust,

unreasonable, unduly discriminatory, or insufficiently reviewed long-term costs on AEP, its

affiliates, and their customers.
